procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 14.05.2010 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRLA No. 1091 of 2005.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court convicted Harbhajan Singh on 18.05.2005 under Section 25 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and sentenced him to 10 years imprisonment. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence on 14.05.2010.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Harbhajan Singh appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order upholding his conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgments passed by the Courts below.

directions: The bail bonds of the Appellant stand discharge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the owner of a vehicle can be convicted under Section 25 of the NDPS Act solely on the basis of ownership, without the prosecution proving that they knowingly permitted its use for a drug-related offence.

facts: The appellant was the registered owner of a truck from which narcotics were recovered after it was found in an accident.
The appellant was not present at the scene of the accident, nor was he arrested from the spot.
The driver and cleaner of the truck were acquitted because the witnesses who were supposed to identify them turned hostile.
The appellant was convicted by the lower courts solely on the basis that he was the registered owner of the vehicle.
law: Section 25 of the NDPS Act requires that an owner of a vehicle must have 'knowingly' permitted it to be used for a drug offence to be convicted.
The owner's knowledge and consent are a 'sine qua non' (an essential condition) for a conviction under Section 25.
The initial burden of proof is on the prosecution to establish the foundational facts, including that the owner had knowledge of the vehicle's illegal use.
The presumption of a 'culpable mental state' under Section 35 of the NDPS Act can only be invoked after the prosecution has discharged its initial burden of proof.
application: The Court found that the prosecution failed to produce any material evidence to prove that the appellant knew his vehicle was being used for transporting narcotics.
It determined that convicting the appellant merely because he was the registered owner was an error, as ownership alone does not establish knowledge.
The Court noted that the lower courts had incorrectly shifted the onus onto the appellant to prove his innocence without the prosecution first proving the foundational facts.
Since the prosecution failed to establish the appellant's knowledge, the presumption under Section 35 could not be applied against him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the owner of a vehicle cannot be convicted under Section 25 of the NDPS Act based on ownership alone. The prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the owner knowingly permitted the vehicle to be used for a drug-related offence. Since the prosecution failed to do so, the appellant's conviction was not legally sustainable and was set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act can be applied against an accused when the prosecution has failed to discharge its initial burden of proving the foundational facts.

facts: The appellant was the registered owner of a truck that was found carrying narcotic substances after it was involved in an accident.
The appellant was not present at the scene, nor was he arrested from the spot.
The driver and cleaner of the truck were identified by two witnesses, but these witnesses later turned hostile in court.
As a result, the driver and cleaner were acquitted.
The appellant was convicted by the lower courts solely on the basis of being the registered owner of the vehicle.
law: Section 25 of the NDPS Act requires that for an owner of a vehicle to be convicted, the prosecution must prove that the owner "knowingly" permitted the vehicle to be used for committing an offence.
Section 35 of the NDPS Act establishes a presumption of a "culpable mental state" (which includes knowledge) on the part of the accused.

Citing precedents like *Noor Aga v. State of Punjab*, the Court clarified that this presumption under Section 35 is not automatic. It can only be invoked after the prosecution has first discharged its initial burden of proving the foundational facts of the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Court found that the prosecution failed to produce any material evidence to show that the appellant had knowledge of or consented to his truck being used for illegal activity.
The appellant's conviction was based only on his ownership of the truck, which the Court stated was insufficient to establish knowledge of its misuse.
Since the prosecution failed to prove the foundational fact—that the owner "knowingly" permitted the vehicle's use for the crime as required by Section 25—the initial burden was not met.
Consequently, the Court determined that the presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 could not be applied against the appellant.
The lower courts had erred by shifting the onus onto the appellant to prove his innocence without the prosecution first establishing the necessary foundational facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act cannot be applied against an accused if the prosecution has failed to discharge its initial burden of proving the foundational facts. In this case, because the prosecution did not prove that the owner knowingly permitted his vehicle to be used for a crime, the presumption was not available, the onus did not shift to the accused, and the conviction was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the owner of a vehicle can be convicted under Section 25 of the NDPS Act solely on the basis of ownership, without the prosecution proving that they knowingly permitted its use for a drug-related offence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was convicted merely on the ground that he was the registered owner of the truck.
The prosecution failed to produce any material evidence to prove that the offence was committed with the knowledge and consent of the appellant.
The appellant was not with the vehicle nor was he arrested from the spot when the contraband was seized.
respondent_arguments: The owner of the truck is vicariously liable for its use in illegal activities.
The appellant failed to prove his claim that the truck was being used for a legitimate purpose (carrying sand).
It is improbable that the driver and cleaner would risk smuggling a large quantity of contraband without the owner's connivance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act can be applied against an accused when the prosecution has failed to discharge its initial burden of proving the foundational facts.
appellant_arguments: The presumption under Section 35 is not available to the prosecution because it failed to discharge its initial burden of proving the foundational facts.
The prosecution did not prove that the vehicle was used for an illegal activity with the knowledge and consent of the appellant.
In the absence of the prosecution proving foundational facts, the onus to prove innocence does not shift to the accused.
respondent_arguments: The presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the Act goes against the appellant.
The High Court was correct to draw a presumption against the appellant under Section 35.

cases.case_name: Bhola Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Regarding the sine qua non (essential condition) for the applicability of Section 25 of the NDPS Act.

cases.case_name: Noor Aga v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: The presumption and reverse burden under Section 35 of the NDPS Act comes into play only after the prosecution has discharged the initial burden to prove the foundational facts.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The presumption under Section 35 of the NDPS Act, which places a reverse burden on an accused, is not available to the prosecution, and the onus will not shift to the accused, if the prosecution fails to first discharge its initial burden of proving the foundational facts.
obiter: For the purpose of this section, a fact is said to be proved only when the court believes it to exist beyond a reasonable doubt and not merely when its existence is established by a preponderance of probability.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The primary error committed by the Courts below while convicting the Appellant is that the onus is sought to be shifted on him to prove his innocence without the foundational facts having been proved by the prosecution. The prosecution failed to produce any material on record to show that the vehicle in question was used for any illegal activity with the knowledge and consent of the Appellant, and in the absence of such proof, the presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act is not available to the prosecution.
legal_tests_applied: For Section 25 of the NDPS Act to apply, the prosecution must first prove the foundational facts that the vehicle was used for an illegal activity with the knowledge and consent of the owner.

The presumption of a culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act is not available to the prosecution if it has failed to discharge the initial burden of proving the foundational facts of the offence.
In the absence of the prosecution proving the foundational facts, the onus to prove innocence does not shift to the accused.
Mere ownership or registration of a vehicle cannot, by itself, fasten the owner with the knowledge of its misuse by others.
policy_considerations: It is a fundamental principle of criminal law that the prosecution must prove its case and establish the foundational facts before the burden of proof can be shifted to the accused to prove their innocence.
